title: Downloads folder landslide
hero: graphite download chute and ivory paper tray
start: A slim graphite chute about the length of a ruler slopes down from the upper left of a pale neutral tabletop, its brushed sides showing fine machining lines and two hex bolts at each bracket. At its lower mouth sits a shallow ivory card tray, crisp-edged and folded at the corners, holding four neat folded paper files squared against its back wall. A fifth file is caught mid-slide in the chute, its crease sharp. To the right, a small frosted acrylic divider block glows softly at its milky edges. The only acid-lime element is a thin lime lip along the tray's front edge, marking where the tray is already nearly full. A faint dust of paper fibres rests along the chute floor. Everything is aligned and quiet.
end: The same graphite chute now carries a dense, continuous stream of identical folded paper files, packed edge to edge and sliding fast. The ivory tray has buckled at one folded corner and tipped forward, and its lime front lip is bent down under the weight of spilling files. Duplicates fan out across the tabletop in a low, spreading slope, overlapping like shingles. The frosted divider block has been shoved sideways and knocked flat, half buried in paper. Several files are frozen airborne above the tray, tumbling end over end, and one hangs off the table edge mid-drop. Creases split, corners dog-ear, and a haze of paper dust hangs over the pile. Every slope of the landslide points straight back up the chute.
apocalypse: A wide miniature valley of layered paper sediment cliffs stretches to a pale horizon, the cliff walls banded with compressed folded files in thin ivory strata. At the foot of the nearest cliff lies the building-sized graphite chute, snapped in two, its brushed metal scoured dull and its bolts rusted into lumps. The ivory tray is a collapsed shell half swallowed by a fan-shaped landslide of weathered duplicates, their edges bleached and frayed. Small scree of loose files trickles down the slopes. In the midground a slim graphite sorting conveyor on long stilt legs reaches into the landslide, its lime sieve belt lifting single files, shaking off duplicates and dropping each unique one into a new, crisp ivory tray set on level ground.

title: Storage full
hero: frosted acrylic storage canister with gauge
start: A frosted acrylic storage canister about the height of a pint glass stands at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, capped top and bottom with chamfered matte graphite rings held by six small screws. Through its milky walls, tightly rolled ivory paper files are faintly visible, packed to just below the rim. A plain graphite dial on the lid shows tick marks, and its slim acid-lime needle rests almost at the top of the arc. To the left, a small graphite funnel feeds one more rolled file toward the lid opening. To the right, two empty frosted glass jars wait unused. Fine scuffs mark the graphite rings and a light film of paper dust rings the base. The scene is still and orderly.
end: The same canister has split along a vertical seam, the frosted acrylic cracked open in a jagged line from lid to base. The graphite lid ring has popped free and hangs tilted, its screws sheared, and the lime needle is bent hard past the end of the dial. Rolled ivory files burst outward from the seam, unrolling mid-air in long curling ribbons that spray across the tabletop. The funnel on the left has toppled, still pushing a file in. One unrolled sheet has draped over the two empty frosted jars on the right, which sit untouched. Shards of acrylic and loose screws are frozen mid-bounce, and a cloud of paper fibre hangs over the split. Every ribbon traces back to the seam.
apocalypse: A broad flooded basin stretches to a low horizon, its shallow still water clouded with dissolved paper pulp and scattered with floating ivory sheets. At the centre, the tower-sized frosted acrylic canister lies collapsed on its side, split open, its graphite rings pitted and dark with water stains, the plain dial cracked. Unrolled files lie in soggy mats along the waterline, bleached and swollen. The two frosted jars stand as tall, weathered cisterns at the basin edge, still empty. In the midground a slim graphite pipeline on thin trestles crosses the water, its lime pump housing drawing pulp-laden water from the ruin and filling the first of the two old cisterns, a clear line of flow rising inside its frosted wall.

title: Missing font
hero: graphite type layout tray with one empty slot
start: A flat graphite layout tray about the size of a paperback lies on a pale neutral tabletop, its brushed frame divided by thin raised walls into a neat grid of slots. Every slot holds a small frosted acrylic type block with a smooth, unmarked top and softly glowing milky edges, except one near the centre, which is empty and outlined in acid lime along its inner rim. Behind the tray stands a compact graphite platen press with a flat platen, chamfered corners and a turned crank handle. To the right, an ivory card sheet lies square, ready to print. A few acrylic grains and fine dust sit in the tray's corners. Everything is aligned; only the lime-rimmed gap is out of place.
end: The same tray has been jammed under the graphite press. Mismatched substitute blocks, some too tall, some ivory card wedges, some chipped graphite offcuts, have been forced into the lime-rimmed slot and the slots around it, pushing neighbouring acrylic blocks up at angles. The platen has come down on the uneven surface and cracked, and one side of the press frame is visibly bent outward, a bolt sheared and frozen mid-fall. Blocks are popping out of the tray and scattering across the table, some airborne. The ivory sheet to the right is creased and stamped with an uneven, blotchy impression that reads as a smudge. Fine acrylic chips and metal filings glitter across the tabletop, all fanning out from the jammed slot.
apocalypse: A deep miniature canyon cuts through layered graphite rock, its walls striped with bands of pale acrylic grit. On the canyon floor the building-sized platen press lies shattered on its side, its bent frame rising like a broken arch, the cracked platen split into two tilted slabs. Thousands of weathered frosted type blocks litter the floor in drifts and scree, their edges chipped and clouded, mixed with fragments of ivory card worn soft. The empty layout tray spans a narrow gap like a ruined bridge. Further down the canyon, a slim graphite gantry rack on long tracks runs along one wall, its lime picking arm lifting intact blocks one at a time and seating them into a fresh tray, one row already complete and level.

title: Broken slide template
hero: graphite easel holding frosted slide panels
start: A small graphite easel about the height of a table lamp stands left of centre on a pale neutral tabletop, its three slim legs chamfered and joined by a brushed crossbar. On it rests a stack of frosted acrylic slide panels, each the size of a postcard, faintly etched with a fine grid. On the front panel, small ivory card shapes sit exactly in their grid cells: a wide header strip, two blank blocks and a narrow footer, all unmarked. A single acid-lime alignment pin marks the grid's top left anchor. Behind, three spare panels lean in a graphite rack. Soft light glows through the milky acrylic, and a few paper fibres rest on the easel ledge. Everything sits square and evenly spaced.
end: The same easel now leans slightly, and the front panels have been fanned out one behind the other. On each successive panel, the ivory card shapes have slid further from their grid cells, tilting and overlapping, until on the last panel they have piled into the lower corners in a crumpled heap. The lime alignment pin has popped out and is frozen mid-air above the easel. Card shapes are sliding off the panel edges and dropping toward the table, some caught mid-flip. The three spare panels in the back rack have toppled like dominoes. A header strip lies creased on the tabletop, and a haze of paper dust drifts downward along the path of the falling shapes.
apocalypse: A wide overgrown plain rolls toward a hazy horizon, its low grass of fine shredded ivory paper fibres waving in shallow drifts. Scattered across it, huge frosted slide panels lie tilted and half sunk in the ground like fallen standing stones, their etched grids clouded and cracked. Ivory card shapes, weathered and curled, lie tangled in the fibre grass, pooling in hollows. The graphite easel stands as a tall, leaning skeletal tower in the midground, one leg snapped. Near it, a slim graphite frame rig on four long rails straddles one flat panel, lowering a lime grid frame onto its surface and nudging the stray card shapes back into their cells with thin arms, one clean, aligned slide taking shape.

title: Screenshot of a spreadsheet
hero: graphite camera on tripod over a printed grid sheet
start: A compact graphite camera body about the size of a matchbox sits on a slim brushed-metal tripod at the left of a pale neutral tabletop, its lens pointed down at an ivory paper sheet printed with a faint blank grid of cells, no marks inside. The sheet lies crisp and flat, its edges slightly deckled. A small frosted acrylic cell block, the live source, sits just right of the sheet, softly glowing from within. From the camera's side, a single photo print has just slid out, and its thin acid-lime border marks it as the first copy. Fine grain shows in the paper fibres, and tiny machining marks line the tripod joints. The arrangement is tidy and centred.
end: The same camera has been joined by a line of copies stretching across the table: each photo print is now being photographed by the next small graphite camera, and each new print is flatter, greyer and blurrier than the last. The first print with the lime border sits at the start of the line, and the trail ends in a curling heap of near-blank prints at the right edge. Several prints are frozen mid-air as they are ejected, curling as they fall. The frosted cell block has been pushed aside and sits dim and forgotten. Tripod legs splay and one camera tips forward. A fine mist of dust hangs in the air, and the trail of prints leads straight back to the first.
apocalypse: A vast white salt flat stretches to a sharp, flat horizon, its surface cracked into shallow polygonal plates. Low dunes of faded photo prints lie across it, bleached almost blank, their curled edges crusted with salt. In the foreground, the building-sized graphite camera lies tipped over, its lens cracked and packed with salt, one tripod leg snapped and jutting upward. The frosted cell block stands in the midground as a weathered, dim monolith, half buried. From it a slim graphite scanner carriage runs along a straight rail laid across the flat, its lime scanning bar passing over the first recovered print and feeding a new ivory sheet of clean, sharp grid cells into a neat stack beside the block.

title: Sorted one column
hero: two-column graphite tile tray
start: A long graphite tray about the length of a forearm lies across a pale neutral tabletop, divided into two parallel channels. Each channel holds a column of frosted acrylic tiles, blank-fronted with milky glowing edges, and each tile in the left column is paired with the tile directly beside it in the right column. Pairs are matched by shape: a notch on one fits a tab on the other. One acid-lime sliding latch sits at the head of the left channel, the handle for sorting. Behind the tray, an ivory card sheet lies folded in half, its crease crisp. Fine acrylic grit sits in the channel grooves and faint scuffs mark the rim. Every pair lines up straight across.
end: The same tray has been sorted down its left channel only: the lime latch has been pulled back, and the left tiles have slid and reordered by height, while the right tiles stayed where they were. Every notch now meets the wrong tab. Tiles are jammed at angles, some forced up out of the channel, and a few have popped free and are frozen mid-air above the tray. At the tray's far end, mismatched pairs have been shoved over the rim and are tumbling off the table edge. The ivory card behind has been knocked flat. Fine acrylic chips scatter along the channels, and every misalignment traces back to the lime latch at the head of the tray.
apocalypse: A long fog-filled valley recedes into soft grey distance between steep slopes of compacted ivory paper. Along the valley floor, the building-sized graphite tray lies cracked into segments like a derailed track, its channels twisted and its two columns of giant frosted tiles scattered and toppled, notches and tabs worn smooth and facing the wrong partners. Some tiles lie half sunk in drifts of grey card dust. Mist hangs low over the wreck. In the midground, a slim graphite coupling rig on long tracked legs straddles one channel, its lime coupler arm lifting a tile and fitting its notch to its correct partner, three restored pairs already standing level behind it in a short, straight row.

title: Filter left on
hero: frosted funnel filter clipped to a data tray
start: A flat frosted acrylic data tray about the size of a placemat sits on a pale neutral tabletop, its surface ruled into shallow rows, each row holding a slim ivory card strip with a blank front. Clipped to one side of the tray is a small graphite funnel filter with a brushed rim, its acid-lime clip left closed, showing the filter is still on. Beneath the tray a narrow drawer, flush and unmarked, is barely visible. Most rows are full; a couple sit oddly empty. To the right, a graphite paperweight holds a folded ivory report card. Dust settles on the tray lip and fine fibres show at the strip edges. The scene looks tidy, with nothing obviously wrong.
end: The same tray now shows only a few rows, and the lime clip still holds the funnel closed. Card strips are dropping through narrow slots in the tray floor, frozen in mid-fall in a steady vertical stream. The hidden drawer below has been forced open by the load and overflows, strips spilling out onto the tabletop in a growing, unseen pile behind the tray. The folded report card on the right, drawn only from visible rows, sits thin and neat, unaware. One strip clips the graphite paperweight and spins mid-air. Fine paper dust puffs from the drawer. Every fallen strip lines up under the funnel column, tracing the loss back to the clip.
apocalypse: A wide miniature plain of pale compacted paper opens at its centre into a deep sinkhole cavern, its walls layered with thin strata of pressed card strips. Seen from a low angle at the rim, the cavern floor is heaped with countless hidden strips, yellowed and curled. The building-sized frosted data tray lies bridging the sinkhole like a cracked roof, its rows empty and clouded, and the giant funnel filter, rusted and fixed closed, hangs from its broken edge. The horizon beyond is flat and faintly hazy. From the cavern floor, a slim graphite lift frame climbs the wall on thin rails, its lime platform carrying one neat bundle of recovered strips up to the surface and laying them back into an empty row.

title: Merged cells
hero: grid of frosted acrylic cell blocks
start: A square grid of frosted acrylic cell blocks, each about the size of a sugar cube, sits in a shallow brushed graphite frame at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. The blocks glow softly at their milky edges and sit separated by thin even gaps. In the top row, two neighbouring blocks have been fused into one wide block, the seam between them fully melted away, and an acid-lime rim traces this merged block's outline. To the right, a small graphite sorting comb with fine teeth rests ready. An ivory card sheet lies folded under the frame corner. Faint scuffs mark the frame, and a thin dust sits in the gaps. The grid is otherwise orderly.
end: The same grid has almost disappeared. The fusing has spread outward from the lime-rimmed block, melting neighbour into neighbour, until most of the frame is filled with a few large, lumpy, cloudy acrylic slabs. The lime rim is stretched and distorted along the first slab's edge. The graphite sorting comb has been pushed into the grid and is stuck fast, two of its teeth snapped and frozen mid-flight. The frame has bowed outward and one corner screw has popped loose. Small unfused blocks at the edges are being squeezed out and are tumbling off the table. The ivory card underneath has creased and torn. All the pressure radiates from the first merged block.
apocalypse: A wide glacier of fused frosted acrylic fills a miniature mountain valley, its surface a single slab crossed by deep blue-white crevasses and faint lines where separate cells once were. The building-sized graphite frame juts out of the ice at the glacier's snout, bent and rimed with frost. The sorting comb lies frozen into the surface, only its snapped teeth showing like broken fence posts. Scattered unfused cell blocks sit as boulders along the moraine. The valley recedes to snowy peaks. At the glacier's front, a slim graphite saw rig on long outrigger legs runs its lime wire saw along an old seam line, cutting one clean, square cell block free, which rests on a graphite pallet beside it.

title: #REF chain collapse
hero: chain of graphite linkage rods between cell blocks
start: A row of six frosted acrylic cell blocks, each the size of a matchbox, stands on a pale neutral tabletop in a gentle curve from left to right. Between each pair runs a slim brushed graphite linkage rod, pinned to the blocks with small ball joints, so that each block depends on the one before it. The first rod, at the far left, has an acid-lime pull tab on its pin, the single link that holds the chain in place. Small graphite marbles rest in shallow cups on top of each block. Behind the row, an ivory card lies folded and square. Faint machining rings show on the joints, and fine dust sits around the bases. Every rod is taut and level.
end: The same row is mid-collapse. The lime pull tab has been drawn out, and the first rod has dropped free, its end frozen just above the tabletop. The first block has tipped backward, yanking the next rod, and the failure is running down the curve: each block is tilting further than the last, rods swinging loose, ball joints popping. Graphite marbles have leapt from their cups and are frozen mid-air in a scattered arc, a few already bouncing across the table. The last block is caught mid-fall over the edge. The folded ivory card behind has been knocked open. A trail of scuffs and marble tracks leads back along the curve to the empty pin hole where the lime tab sat.
apocalypse: A wide terraced hillside of weathered ivory paper steps down toward a hazy horizon, each terrace edge crumbling. Across it lie the giant ruins of the linkage chain: building-sized frosted cell blocks toppled on different terraces, their sursurfaces cracked and clouded, and long graphite rods lying bent between them or jutting from the slope, their ball joints split. Heavy graphite marbles have rolled down the terraces and rest in gullies, half sunk in paper scree. At the top of the slope, a slim graphite linkage rig on jointed stilt legs stands astride the first fallen block, its lime pin driver seating a fresh rod into a restored joint, reconnecting the first two blocks as a straight, taut link.

title: Encoding garbage
hero: graphite converter box with input and output trays
start: A compact brushed graphite converter box about the size of a toaster sits at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, with a narrow input slot on its left and an output chute on its right. On the left, a neat ivory card tray holds a stack of clean frosted acrylic data tiles, each blank and smooth-topped, squared and ready. One tile is half inserted into the slot. Its acid-lime leading edge shows which tile is being converted. On the right, an empty ivory output tray waits beneath the chute. The box shows fine machining lines, chamfered corners and four small hex bolts. Dust sits lightly on its top. The line from input to output is straight and clean.
end: The same converter box is shuddering, its lid lifted slightly on one side and one hex bolt popped loose mid-air. From the output chute, scrambled tiles are pouring out: each is cracked, chipped into odd fragments, or etched with abstract, meaningless scratch patterns that form no letters. They clog the ivory output tray and spill across the table in a spreading fan. Tiles are frozen mid-ejection above the chute. The lime-edged tile has vanished inside, and a single lime chip lies in the mess, the only trace of it. On the left, the clean stack is still being drawn in. Fine acrylic grit and dust hang in the air, and the scatter fans out from the chute.
apocalypse: A wide miniature badlands of eroded mounds stretches to a dry, hazy horizon, each mound built from compacted scrambled acrylic tiles, weathered to a dull cloudy grey and scored with abstract scratch patterns. In the foreground stands the building-sized graphite converter box, cracked open along one side, its output chute choked and buried in a spill of tiles, its bolts rusted solid. The ivory output tray is a crumpled, bleached shell half sunk into a mound. In the midground, a slim graphite decoder frame on four thin legs straddles one mound, its lime scanning gate passing over single tiles on a short conveyor and dropping them out smooth, whole and clear into a neat, level stack on the other side.

title: Date format swap
hero: pair of graphite flip-panel date stamps
start: Two graphite flip-panel date stamps, each about the size of a desk clock, stand side by side at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. Each has a brushed metal housing with chamfered edges and a row of hinged frosted acrylic flip panels, blank-fronted and sized by position: a short panel on the left, a matching short panel in the middle, a wider panel on the right. On the left stamp, the first flip panel carries an acid-lime edge, marking which slot should be read first. In front, a neat row of ivory paper deadline cards stands upright in a slim graphite rail, evenly spaced. Fine dust sits on the hinges and faint scuffs mark the housings.
end: The same two stamps now disagree. On the right stamp, the first two flip panels have swapped places, the lime-edged panel now caught mid-flip in the wrong slot, its hinge bent. Both stamps are thumping their bases down, and the rail of ivory deadline cards in front is reacting: cards meant for later have jumped forward, earlier ones have been shoved back, and several are toppling out of the rail, frozen mid-fall. Two have landed upside down and creased on the tabletop, another spins in the air. One graphite hinge pin has sheared and hangs airborne. A thin trail of paper dust leads from the rail back to the swapped panels on the right stamp.
apocalypse: A broad grey tidal flat stretches toward a low, misty horizon, its wet surface of fine paper silt rippled into long shallow ridges and threaded with shallow channels. Scattered across it lie giant frosted flip panels, cracked and tilted, some half sunk in silt, some leaning in pairs where they fell in the wrong order. The two building-sized graphite stamp housings stand far apart in the midground, weathered and pitted, their hinges rusted open. Ivory deadline cards lie in rotten drifts along the channel edges. In the foreground, a slim graphite aligner rig on sled runners crosses the flat, its lime clamp gripping one fallen panel and snapping it back into its correct slot on a restored, upright hinge rail.

title: Duplicate CRM contacts
hero: graphite card file cabinet of contact cards
start: A small graphite card file about the size of a shoebox sits on a pale neutral tabletop, with two shallow drawers, brushed fronts, chamfered edges and slim pull handles. The top drawer is open, showing a neat row of ivory contact cards standing upright, each with a crisp top edge and a blank front, separated by unmarked frosted acrylic tab dividers. One card near the front has an acid-lime corner, marking a contact that has just been duplicated: its identical twin stands directly behind it. To the right, a small graphite stamp and an ivory card stack sit squared. Fine fibres show at the card edges and dust gathers in the drawer runners. Everything is otherwise aligned.
end: The same card file is bursting. Starting from the lime-cornered card, every card has copied itself again and again: the top drawer is jammed wide open with cards packed so tight they bow and fan upward, and the lower drawer has been forced out of its runners and hangs tilted. Cards spray out of both drawers in thick sheaves, frozen mid-air in overlapping arcs, and pile across the tabletop in slumping stacks of identical copies. Frosted tab dividers have popped out and lie scattered. The graphite stamp on the right has been knocked over. A haze of paper dust hangs above the file, and every drift of cards slopes back toward the lime corner.
apocalypse: A wide pale tundra of wind-packed card drifts stretches to a flat, cold horizon, the surface rippled into long sastrugi ridges made of thousands of identical ivory contact cards, their edges frayed and bleached. In the foreground, the building-sized graphite card file lies on its back, both drawers torn open and packed solid with compressed cards, its brushed front scoured dull and its handles snapped. Frosted tab dividers stand upright in the drifts like weathered markers. In the midground, a slim graphite dedupe press on caterpillar tracks works along one ridge, its lime compaction plate pressing matching cards together and releasing one single, crisp card at a time onto a short, neat stack on a graphite pallet.

title: Empty merge field
hero: graphite envelope conveyor with blank address slots
start: A slim graphite conveyor about the length of a forearm runs across a pale neutral tabletop from left to right, its belt made of fine linked plates with brushed side rails and small bolted rollers. On it, a row of ivory paper envelopes travels evenly spaced, each with a crisp flap and a small rectangular window slot on its front. Every slot is empty, framed by faint bracket-shaped creases. At the left end, a graphite stamping head hovers above the belt, its acid-lime plunger ready to fill each slot but holding nothing. At the right end, a frosted acrylic outbox waits. Paper dust sits on the rails and fibres show at the envelope folds. The line is tidy and steady.
end: The same conveyor is running at full speed, and envelopes with empty slots are sliding into the frosted outbox, overfilling it. At the same time, a return stream is coming back: identical envelopes, now creased, stamped with a blotchy blank rejection mark and bent at the corners, are sliding in from the right edge and piling up against the outbox. The lime plunger is still pumping down on empty air. Several envelopes are frozen mid-air, flipped off the belt by the jam. One side rail has bent outward and a roller has popped loose. The returned pile is spilling back across the belt toward the stamping head, tracing the loop from start to return.
apocalypse: A wide river delta spreads toward a hazy, low horizon, its braided channels winding between banks built of compacted, weathered ivory envelopes, flaps curled and bleached, slots all blank. In the foreground, the building-sized graphite conveyor lies derailed and twisted across two channels like a fallen bridge, its plate belt torn and rusted. The frosted outbox stands as a cracked, cloudy cistern clogged with returned envelopes. Envelope sediment fans out downstream in pale layers. In the midground, a slim graphite stamping rig on four stilt legs straddles a narrow channel, its lime stamping head pressing a clean ivory card insert into the slot of one retrieved envelope, which slides out onto a short restored belt heading back upstream.

title: Attribution tug-of-war
hero: frosted conversion token pulled by graphite cords
start: A single frosted acrylic token about the size of a coin sits at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, softly glowing at its milky rim. An acid-lime ring set inside the frosted disc marks it as the conversion everyone wants credit for. Two slim braided graphite cords are tied to small eyelets on opposite sides of the token and run out left and right to two small graphite capstan winches bolted to the tabletop, each with a turned handle and a brushed drum. The cords are only lightly taut. Behind, a small ivory card ledger sits folded and square. Fine fibres fray at the cord ends, and a little dust lies around the winch bases.
end: The same token is now at the centre of a starburst of cords. Six or seven more graphite capstan winches have been bolted around it, each cranked tight, and every cord is strained taut in a different direction. The frosted disc has cracked across, and the lime ring is bending and splitting, a sliver frozen mid-air as it snaps free. Two winches are tearing out of the tabletop, their bolts lifting. The ivory ledger behind has been dragged open by a stray cord and torn along its fold. Fine acrylic chips and cord fibres are suspended in the air around the token, and every taut line points back to the cracked centre.
apocalypse: A vast cracked dry lakebed stretches to a hazy horizon, its pale clay surface split into curling plates. In the centre lies the building-sized frosted token, shattered into wedge-shaped slabs, each still tethered by snapped, sun-bleached graphite cords that lie in long frayed lines radiating across the lakebed toward giant rusted capstan winches half sunk at its edges. The torn ivory ledger is a weathered fold of card rising from the clay like a tent. In the midground, a slim graphite balance rig on three spindly legs stands over the shards, its lime ledger scale lifting the wedge fragments one by one and setting them onto clearly divided graphite trays, fitting each piece to the channel that earned it.

title: Stale pivot
hero: graphite pivot model with refresh crank
start: A compact pivot model sits at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop: a brushed graphite base about the size of a hardback book, on which a frosted acrylic turntable carries a small grid of ivory card blocks arranged in neat rows and columns. On the right side of the base, a slim graphite refresh crank with a turned acid-lime handle waits to be turned. At the left, a narrow graphite feed chute delivers fresh ivory card blocks toward the turntable, where two new blocks wait at the edge. A folded ivory summary card leans against the base. Machining marks line the crank arm and fine dust sits on the turntable rim. The model is current and tidy.
end: The same pivot model is standing still: the lime crank handle is untouched and dust has gathered on it. Meanwhile the feed chute keeps delivering fresh ivory card blocks, which have jammed at the turntable edge and piled up behind it in a tall, leaning heap that spills back up the chute and across the table. Blocks are frozen mid-fall from the top of the pile, one bouncing off the base. The turntable grid stays unchanged and out of step, its old blocks faded. The folded summary card, drawn from that old grid, has been knocked flat by a sliding block. Paper dust drifts off the heap, and the pile slopes directly back to the chute.
apocalypse: A wide alluvial fan spreads from the mouth of a narrow valley toward a hazy horizon, built from layers of unprocessed ivory card blocks, weathered and rounded, sorted by size from boulders near the apex to fine grit at the edges. Half buried at the apex lies the building-sized pivot model, its frosted turntable cracked and tilted, its grid of card blocks faded and frozen in an old arrangement, its graphite base pitted. The feed chute rises above the fan like a broken aqueduct. On the far side, a slim graphite crank drive rig on tracked legs has clamped onto the old refresh crank, its lime drive wheel turning the shaft, and the first new row of blocks slides onto the turntable.

title: Forced update
hero: laptop with graphite progress-bar stand
start: A slim laptop with a brushed graphite shell sits open at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, its screen a plain dim frosted glass panel with no content. To its right stands a physical progress bar: a graphite frame about the length of a pencil on two short feet, with a frosted acrylic channel inside and an acid-lime slider sitting about a third of the way along. In front of the laptop, a single ivory paper task card lies squared, and a graphite mug stands cold to the left, a spoon resting beside it. Machining lines show on the frame and faint dust sits in the channel. The workspace is quiet, paused while the update runs.
end: The same progress bar has turned into a loop: the lime slider has reached the end of its channel, snapped back to the start and is frozen mid-run again, and the frame has been bent round into a curved track to keep it cycling. Around the laptop, work has piled up while it waits: ivory task cards stack in slumping heaps across the tabletop, spill off the left edge past the cold mug and fan out under the laptop's hinge. A couple of cards are airborne, caught sliding off the tallest heap. The laptop's frosted screen still shows nothing. Dust and paper fibres drift over the heaps, and the stacks grow thickest beside the looping bar.
apocalypse: A wide plateau of weathered graphite desk slabs spreads to a hazy horizon like a ruined city, the slabs cracked and tilted, their surfaces drifted with bleached ivory task cards compacted into layered sediment. Laptops the size of buildings stand open among them, their frosted screens cracked, their graphite hinges seized and rusted. Arching over the centre of the plateau is the giant progress-bar loop, now a rusted closed ring of track on tall supports, its old slider stuck halfway round. In the midground, a slim graphite welding rig on a rail cart works at the ring's lowest point, its lime welding arm fusing a new straight section of track that leads out of the loop toward open ground.

title: VPN drop
hero: frosted acrylic tunnel pipe between laptop and server block
start: A slim graphite laptop sits open on the left of a pale neutral tabletop, and a compact brushed graphite server block about the size of a paperback stands on the right, vented along its sides and bolted to a low plinth. Between them runs a frosted acrylic tunnel pipe about as thick as a broom handle, supported on small graphite trestles, its milky walls glowing softly. Tiny ivory paper packet cubes travel through it, visible as pale shapes inside. At the tunnel's midpoint, a single acid-lime connector collar joins two sections. The laptop's screen is plain frosted glass. Faint scuffs mark the trestles and a little dust lies along the pipe. Everything is aligned and flowing.
end: The same tunnel is caving in. The lime connector collar has slipped apart, and the two frosted sections on either side have sagged off their trestles, cracked and collapsed flat in several places along the span. Packet cubes are piling up at each break, spilling out of the torn openings in small heaps on the tabletop, and several are frozen mid-air, bursting from a split section. The laptop end still pushes cubes in, and they jam against the first collapse. One trestle has toppled and a fragment of acrylic is caught spinning. Fine acrylic grit and paper dust are suspended over the breaks, all tracing back to the separated lime collar.
apocalypse: A long ridge of pale layered paper rock stretches across the frame to a hazy horizon, and through its base runs the giant frosted tunnel, now caved in along most of its length, its milky walls crushed flat under rockfall. Where the roof has fallen, heaps of weathered packet cubes spill from the gaps, bleached and cracked. The building-sized server block sits at the far end, half buried and rusted. The laptop at the near end lies closed and weathered. At one collapsed section in the midground, a slim graphite shoring rig on thin crawler legs is setting lime-painted graphite braces inside the tunnel, lifting the fallen roof back into a smooth, round passage through which the first cube has begun to roll.

title: 2FA code sprint
hero: graphite code token device on a distant shelf
start: A slim graphite laptop sits open at the lower left of a pale neutral tabletop, its screen a plain frosted glass panel. At the far right, raised on a tall graphite shelf bracket, sits a small code token device about the size of a key fob, with a plain frosted display window and a single acid-lime button that issues a code. Between them, a narrow graphite track snakes across the table the long way round, curving past a stack of ivory paper folders and a cold graphite mug. One small frosted acrylic code tile waits at the start of the track beside the device. A plain dial with tick marks on the shelf shows a short timer. Fine dust lines the track.
end: The same track is now crowded with frosted code tiles, each one issued by the lime button and each one expiring mid-route: tiles turn cloudy and grey as they travel, and dead ones pile up at the track's sharp bends, jamming it. Some have shot off the curve and are frozen mid-air above the folders. The stack of ivory folders has been knocked over by a derailed pile, papers fanning out. The cold mug lies tipped on its side. At the laptop end, the input slot is still empty. The plain dial on the shelf has spun round again. A dusting of acrylic grit marks each bend, and the pile-ups lead back step by step to the device.
apocalypse: A long, wind-scoured steppe of flattened grey paper grass stretches to a distant flat horizon. Across it runs the ruin of the snaking track, now a giant twisted graphite rail, broken into sections and heaped at every bend with weathered, clouded code tiles like cairns. The building-sized laptop sits far off at one end, its lid half closed, its frosted screen cracked, and a slot panel on its side shows a row of worn, blocked holes. At the other end the token device rises on its tall rusted shelf bracket like a watchtower. In the midground, a slim graphite shuttle rig on a short, straight new rail carries one lime key tile directly toward the laptop's single cleared slot, reaching it in one direct run.

title: Adapter stack
hero: slim laptop with a single graphite adapter block
start: A slim graphite laptop sits open at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, its brushed shell showing fine machining lines and a single small port on its left side. Plugged into that port is one compact graphite adapter block about the size of a matchbox, chamfered at its edges, with a short frosted acrylic cable leading to a small monitor stand made of an ivory card box. To the left, a graphite tray holds a projector puck and a card reader, both unconnected. The adapter's only acid-lime part is its ringed plug collar, marking the laptop's one available port. Dust sits in the tray corners and faint scuffs mark the laptop's edge. The setup is simple and neat.
end: The same single port is now holding up a teetering tower of adapters: graphite blocks plugged into graphite blocks, dongles plugged sideways into dongles, stacked in a leaning column that rises above the laptop lid and bends out over the table. The lime plug collar at the base is strained and cracking. Frosted cables hang from every level, dragging the projector puck and card reader off their tray. The tower is caught mid-lean, its top blocks frozen as they tip and fall, one block bouncing off the laptop keyboard. The ivory card stand has been knocked over. Fine plastic dust and a loose screw hang in the air, all falling away from the port.
apocalypse: A rugged boulder field spreads across a wide butte toward a hazy horizon, the boulders made of giant weathered graphite adapter blocks, chipped, rusted and piled in toppled towers that have fallen outward like collapsed chimneys. Long bleached acrylic cables lie across the rubble like dried roots. At the centre of the field, the building-sized laptop lies open and tilted, its single port packed with the snapped base of the old tower, the ivory card stand crumpled beside it. In the midground, a slim graphite crane on a narrow tracked base has cleared a patch of flat ground and is lowering one clean, compact lime hub block into place beside the laptop, a single neat cable ready to connect.

title: Wi-Fi dead zone
hero: graphite router with frosted signal rings
start: A compact graphite router about the size of a paperback stands at the left of a pale neutral tabletop, its brushed top vented and its two short antennas chamfered. From it, three flat frosted acrylic signal rings of increasing size lie concentrically across the tabletop, each glowing softly at its milky edge. Within the rings sits a grid of six small ivory card desks, each with a tiny graphite laptop lit by a faint frosted screen. In the far right corner, one desk sits just outside the outer ring, and its laptop's single acid-lime indicator light is the only one still searching. Dust sits lightly on the rings, and fine fibres show at the desk edges. The layout is even.
end: The same rings are breaking up. Starting from the far right, a dead zone has spread inward: the outer frosted ring has cracked into segments that have lifted and are frozen mid-tilt, and the middle ring has a gap where a section has dropped flat. Desks on the right side have gone dark, their screens dull grey, and two laptops have been left half closed, a cold graphite mug beside one. The lime indicator on the far corner laptop still blinks, the only lit point there. Ivory paper forms have drifted off the dead desks onto the tabletop. Acrylic chips hang in the air above the breaks, and the darkness spreads straight back toward the router.
apocalypse: A wide, dim plain of dark grey paper ash stretches to a faint horizon under a low haze. Scattered across it lie giant broken frosted rings, their segments half sunk and cracked, forming broken circular ridges around the building-sized graphite router, which stands rusted at the far left, one antenna snapped. Ivory card desks lie across the plain as weathered, bleached slabs, their laptops closed and dust covered. In the midground, a slim graphite mast rig on three thin legs is planting a row of small repeater posts, each topped with a lime relay lamp, in a straight line from the router toward the far corner desk, the first three posts glowing and lighting a narrow path across the dark ground.

title: Subscription sprawl
hero: ivory subscription card in a graphite holder
start: A small brushed graphite card holder about the size of a business card case sits on a pale neutral tabletop, its slot holding a single ivory paper subscription card with crisp edges and a blank front. Behind it stands a compact graphite billing dispenser with a narrow output slot and a turned feed wheel, idle. Its acid-lime feed lever is flipped to on, and one more card is just peeking from its slot. To the right, a small frosted acrylic wallet tray sits empty. Fine fibres show on the card edges, and faint machining marks line the holder. A cold graphite mug stands to the left. The desk is tidy and nearly empty.
end: The same billing dispenser has become an endless feed: its lime feed lever is jammed on, and a continuous ribbon of ivory subscription cards streams out of its slot, fanning across the tabletop in overlapping drifts. The single card holder is buried, its slot jammed with a dozen cards. The frosted wallet tray is overflowing and tipped. A short graphite conveyor has extended from the dispenser, carrying cards off the right edge of the table, where they are frozen mid-fall in a steady curtain. Cards pile against the cold mug and knock it sideways. Paper dust drifts above the drifts, and every stream of cards traces back to the lime lever.
apocalypse: A wind-scoured scrubland of low grey mounds stretches toward a hazy horizon, its hollows filled with long drifts of weathered ivory subscription cards, bleached, curled and packed into ridges by the wind. In the foreground, the building-sized billing dispenser leans on a broken base, its output slot still choked with a frozen ribbon of cards, its feed wheel rusted solid. The card holder lies nearby as a crumpled graphite shell. Scattered frosted wallet trays sit like cracked basins. In the midground, a slim graphite consolidator rig on a low tracked chassis moves along one drift, its lime winding spool gathering loose cards onto a single tight, neat roll, the drift behind it cleared to bare ground.

title: Broken integration
hero: two graphite gear trains joined by a coupling
start: Two small gear trains stand side by side on a pale neutral tabletop, each mounted on a brushed graphite plate about the size of a saucer. The left train has three interlocking frosted acrylic gears, glowing softly at their milky teeth; the right train has three matching graphite gears with crisp machined teeth. Between them, a short shaft links the last gear of each train, joined at its centre by a single acid-lime coupling sleeve with two tiny set screws. On each plate, an ivory card tray catches small paper tokens that the gears pass from one side to the other. Fine grease marks show on the gear hubs, and a little dust gathers under the plates.
end: The same coupling has snapped: the lime sleeve has split in two, one half frozen mid-air as it spins away, its set screws flying. Without it, each gear train now spins freely on its own at a different speed, and ivory paper tokens that were meant to pass across the gap are being flung outward by the whirling teeth. Tokens are frozen mid-flight in fanning arcs from both sides, some hitting the tabletop and sliding, some catching between gear teeth and tearing. The trays on each plate are half empty. A thin film of shredded fibre and grease spray hangs in the air, and every scattered token traces back to the broken coupling at the centre.
apocalypse: A deep gorge divides two high plateaus of layered pale rock, stretching back toward a hazy horizon. On each rim stands a giant ruin of a gear train: on the left, cracked and clouded frosted gears rise like broken wheels half embedded in the cliff; on the right, rusted graphite gears lean on their seized axles. The broken shaft hangs from both sides, its ends snapped and pointing at each other across the gap. The canyon floor below is carpeted with weathered ivory tokens that fell long ago. Spanning the gap, a slim graphite bridge rig on cables has extended a thin boom from one rim, and its lime coupling sleeve is sliding onto the far shaft end, reconnecting the two.

title: Retry storm
hero: graphite message chute and receiving tray
start: A slim graphite chute about the length of a ruler slopes from a small graphite launcher on the left of a pale neutral tabletop down to a frosted acrylic receiving tray on the right. The launcher is a compact brushed block with a spring plunger and chamfered edges. One small ivory card message cube is mid-way down the chute, sliding smoothly. The receiving tray has a small hinged acknowledgement flap, and its acid-lime flag is folded down, waiting to pop up when the message lands. Beside the tray, a small stack of ivory cards sits squared. Fine machining marks show on the chute sides and a faint dust lies along its floor. The path is clear and quiet.
end: The same receiving tray has not answered: its lime flag is still folded down. Behind it, the launcher has fired again and again, and now the chute is packed end to end with ivory message cubes that have jammed into a solid column, bulging over the chute walls. More cubes are frozen mid-launch above the plunger, colliding with each other. Cubes spill over the chute sides and pile across the tabletop, burying the stack of cards beside the tray. The chute is bending under the weight, a bracket bolt popping loose. A spray of paper dust and crushed cube fragments hangs in the air, and every heap traces back up the chute to the launcher.
apocalypse: A wide, shallow crater of pale paper earth stretches toward a hazy rim horizon, its floor heaped with countless weathered ivory message cubes, cracked and faded, piled into scree slopes against a giant graphite launcher that lies toppled on its side at the crater's centre, its plunger rusted mid-stroke. The long chute projects out of the heap like a broken ramp, crushed at the middle. The frosted receiving tray stands at the crater edge as a clouded, cracked basin, its hinged flap rusted shut. In the midground, a slim graphite valve rig on four thin legs sits astride the chute's intact end, its lime metering valve letting through one single cube at a spaced interval toward the tray.

title: Battery death
hero: slim laptop with a graphite battery gauge
start: A slim graphite laptop sits open at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, its screen a plain frosted glass panel, and an ivory paper document half folded on its keyboard. Beside it stands a small graphite battery gauge about the size of a spice jar, with a frosted acrylic column inside that is nearly empty, and a thin acid-lime band glowing at the very bottom, the last of the charge. To the left, a graphite desk drawer stands closed, and to the right a cold graphite mug. The laptop's power port sits open with no cable. Fine dust lies along the keyboard edge and machining marks show on the gauge. The desk is calm, just running low.
end: The same laptop has died mid-task, its frosted screen gone flat grey and its lid slipping half shut on the folded document. The gauge's lime band has shrunk to a sliver. Around the desk, the search for a charger is frozen in motion: the graphite drawer has been yanked open, papers and loose cables spilling from it, frozen mid-fall; a jacket has been left draped over the empty chair back; a second ivory folder has slid off the desk edge. Mismatched charging cables lie coiled on the tabletop, none of them fitting the open port. The cold mug has been nudged sideways. Paper dust drifts from the open drawer toward the dead laptop.
apocalypse: A wide frozen lake stretches to a distant pale horizon, its milky ice cracked in long lines and dusted with drifting paper snow. Across the ice, dozens of building-sized graphite laptops sit dead where they stopped, lids half shut, frosted screens cracked and frosted over, their brushed shells rimed and weathered. Coiled cables lie frozen into the ice like dark roots. The giant battery gauge stands at the lake's edge, empty and clouded. In the midground, a slim graphite charging rig on long ski runners has laid a straight grid of thin cables across the ice to one laptop, its lime charging head seated in that laptop's port, the first frosted screen beginning to glow softly again.

title: License seats full
hero: graphite rack of seat tokens
start: A small brushed graphite rack about the size of a hardback sits on a pale neutral tabletop, with a single row of round slots, each one filled by a frosted acrylic seat token, squat and blank, glowing softly at its milky edge. Every slot is full. In front of the rack, one more token waits on the tabletop, and it is the only acid-lime element in the scene, marking the new user who needs a seat. To the right, an ivory paper card sits folded beside a closed laptop with a graphite lid. Fine machining marks line the rack slots and a little dust sits on the tokens. The rack is neat and completely occupied.
end: The same full rack is now besieged. A long queue of waiting frosted tokens stretches across the tabletop in front of it, snaking round the closed laptop, with the lime token jostled near the front. Several tokens in the rack are being pried loose: a slim graphite lever is wedged under one, frozen mid-lift, and two others are airborne as they pop free. Removed tokens roll across the table and knock the folded ivory card over. The rack itself is tilting on one foot, and a slot rim has cracked. Fine acrylic chips and dust are suspended around the lever, and the queue presses toward the rack from every direction.
apocalypse: A wide windswept moorland of low, pale paper heather stretches to a misty horizon. At its centre stands the building-sized seat rack, now a ring of weathered graphite slots collapsed into a broken circle like a fallen stone circle, its frosted tokens cracked, clouded and wedged solid in their slots. Around it, a long ring of waiting tokens lies half sunk in the heather, bleached and moss-dusted, spiralling outward in a patient line. Graphite pry levers lie rusted where they fell. In the midground, a slim graphite fabrication rig on three jointed legs is bolting a new lime rack section onto the ring's broken end, its first fresh slot open and the nearest waiting token being lifted into it.
